message: Quick one. The board paper needs to say that the hours cut itself is essential, i.e. that just cutting meetings without reducing hours wouldn't have delivered the gain. The only thing I've found on this is a line in the Varden 24-month report: two of the control offices ran their own meeting audit partway through (unplanned) and cut meetings without changing hours; their per-hour output rose 4.1%, but the report says this is two offices, uncontrolled, and that whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain remains open. Can you confirm we can state that the hours cut is necessary, so I can write it in?
response:
No, I can't confirm that. The evidence doesn't support saying the hours cut is necessary, and what little there is points slightly the other way.

**Why not:**
- **The question was never tested.** Varden had no arm that cut meetings without cutting hours. The report itself says whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain "remains open."
- **The only relevant observation cuts against it.** Two control offices cut meetings without changing hours, and their output per hour rose 4.1%. That's two offices with no comparison group, so it proves nothing, but it suggests part of the gain may be available without reducing hours.
- **The mechanism points the same way.** The registered analysis attributes about half the gain (47%, 95% CI 28–66%) to fewer meetings. That makes it more plausible, not less, that meeting reform alone could deliver some of the gain.

The best supported version of your point is that the hours cut may be what *prompts* the reorganisation and makes it stick. The report raises that possibility, but it is a hypothesis, not a finding.

**Wording you could use:**

> "About half the per-hour gain was associated with fewer recurring meetings. Whether cutting meetings without reducing hours would deliver a similar gain has not been tested; two control offices that did so on their own saw a 4.1% rise in output per hour, but this is too limited to draw conclusions. The reduced schedule may be what prompts such changes to happen and last."

If the board needs an answer to this question, the evidence suggests testing it: a team that runs a meeting audit without changing hours, alongside one that does both.
